findings.issue_text: Email validation gated on email_changed? means BlockedEmail check silently never executes on code paths where email_changed? is false, allowing users with blocked emails to pass validation and register

Client shows generic 'user.email.invalid' message for blocked emails instead of a blocked-specific message

BlockedEmail.should_block? uses case-sensitive exact string matching, allowing blocked emails to bypass validation via case variation like Spam@EVIL.com

Refactoring email validations in user.rb made presence and uniqueness checks conditional on email_changed?, weakening previously unconditional invariants and allowing an unchanged-but-cleared email to persist

should_block? performs a read-modify-write incrementing match_count inside model validation, causing double-counting when valid? and save both run validation, and silently mutating stats on read-only validation paths
match_count += 1 is a lost-update race: concurrent signups with the same blocked email can lose increments due to no atomic UPDATE or FOR UPDATE guard

For genuinely blocked emails, client discards the server's specific reason and substitutes generic user.email.invalid message, making blocked and typo'd emails indistinguishable in the form
Blocked email check inside EmailValidator is gated by if: :email_changed?, so blocked emails pass validation when email is unchanged, narrowing enforcement without documented intent

Replacing validates_presence_of/uniqueness_of with a single validates call gates presence and uniqueness on email_changed?, removing the unconditional presence/uniqueness guarantee for unchanged emails

Case-sensitive blocklist lookup in BlockedEmail.where(email: email) allows blocked emails to be bypassed by capitalizing letters; emails must be normalized (downcased/stripped) at lookup and insertion
should_block? performs a DB read-modify-write (incrementing match_count and saving) inside model validation, enabling unauthenticated write amplification with no rate-limit guard on POST /users
Counter write happens even when other validations fail, so requests creating no account still write to blocked_emails table
Validation can run multiple times per request lifecycle (e.g., valid? called twice), double-incrementing counters

Whitelist/blacklist regex uses substring matching with no anchor or domain-boundary check, so a whitelist entry like @good.com matches anywhere in the string allowing bypass (e.g., user@evil.com@good.com.fake.tld)
Setting value is interpolated into Regexp.new with only dots escaped, allowing regex metacharacters like (, ), {, * to cause ReDoS or malformed-pattern exceptions

EmailValidator whitelist/blacklist logic migrated from User has zero test coverage; spec only stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and never exercises email_domains_whitelist, email_domains_blacklist, or domain-regex escaping branches

Blocked-path tests are tautological against a stub; side-effecting BlockedEmail.should_block? (increments match_count and saves record on every validation attempt including failed/repeat retries) is never tested through the validator

record.errors[attribute].blank? guard is untested; no spec constructs a case where domain-restriction already added an error AND email is blocked, so a flipped boolean adding a wrong second error message would ship silently

New rejectedEmails client-side blocking flow (users_controller + create_account_controller) has no tests anywhere in the diff; payload contract between symbol-keyed errors hash and JS check on result.errors.email may silently never fire, and rejectedEmails dependent-key invalidation/early-return in emailValidation are unverified

BlockedEmail#should_block? performs DB writes (match_count/last_match_at updates via record.save) inside validation, which commits even when the surrounding user save fails, inflating statistics outside the failed transaction

BlockedEmail save errors (e.g. unique-index race under concurrent validation of the same email) raise inside validation, turning a normal signup into a 500 with no retryable path; counter should be incremented after the user save commits
BlockedEmail email matching is case-sensitive (exact-byte where clause) while the legacy blacklist/whitelist regex was case-insensitive, so differently-cased emails like SPAM@X.COM bypass the block

Nothing in the migration, model, or seed path normalizes case when populating blocked_emails, breaking the backfill/import contract; lookup should downcase both sides and the unique index should enforce it

users_controller returns user-controlled email in result.values which the frontend permanently blacklists client-side, showing user.email.invalid for that exact string even when the server-side error was different (not_allowed or uniqueness)
Read-modify-write increment of match_count loses increments under concurrency (last writer wins); should use an atomic UPDATE like update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, ...")

Client pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails whenever any email error (including uniqueness 'already taken') is present, permanently showing 'invalid' message and blocking retry of that email even after correcting a different field
BlockedEmail.should_block? discards the return value of record.save, so failed writes (lost-update race on match_count, lock timeout) silently drop statistics with no logging

Side-effectful DB write on every validation attempt inflates match_count and performs unguarded writes on a read path for repeated form submits, admin email edits, and retries after other validation failures

Email validator's nil handling depends on presence validation firing before the each-validator; any refactor reordering validations would pass nil through email_in_restriction_setting? (latent coupling)

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Email validation gated on email_changed? means BlockedEmail check silently never executes on code paths where email_changed? is false, allowing users with blocked emails to pass validation and register

adjudication.rationale: In `User`, the email validator is still explicitly gated behind `if: :email_changed?` (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`). That gating already existed before this diff (`validate :email_validator, if: :email_changed?`). The new `EmailValidator` adds the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` check, but it will execute whenever the validator runs (i.e., when `email_changed?` is true). The claim that this allows users with blocked emails to “pass validation and register” is not demonstrated by the diff, since new user creation normally sets `email`, making it “changed” and thus triggering the validator.

adjudication_records.issue_text: EmailValidator's validate_each calls value =~ regexp and BlockedEmail.should_block? with unguarded nil value, causing NoMethodError/500 from UsersController#create when email is nil and a whitelist/blacklist setting is present

adjudication.rationale: In `EmailValidator#email_in_restriction_setting?`, `value =~ regexp` is safe even when `value` is nil because Ruby defines `NilClass#=~` (it returns nil, not a NoMethodError). Likewise, `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` will execute `where(email: nil).first` and simply return false without raising. The diff does not show any path where a nil email would cause a NoMethodError/500 in `UsersController#create` due to these calls.

adjudication_records.issue_text: blocked_emails table is created and read but no writer exists (no admin UI, API, rake task, or seed), making the feature unusable without manual SQL

adjudication.rationale: In this diff the new `blocked_emails` table/model (`CreateBlockedEmails` migration, `BlockedEmail` model) is only ever *read* in production code via `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` inside `EmailValidator`, and there is no added admin UI/controller, API endpoint, rake task, seed, or other code path to create/manage `BlockedEmail` records. The only writes shown are internal statistics updates (`match_count`, `last_match_at`) when a matching record already exists, plus test fabrications. That makes the feature dependent on pre-existing/manual population of the table, which is an incomplete product surface rather than a runtime correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs record.save during validation, issuing a DB write on the read path and mutating match_count/last_match_at as a side effect even when validation isn't intended to persist
matched_golden_ids: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both comments flag that the should_block* method performs a write (saving/updating match_count/last_match_at statistics) while ostensibly doing a read/check operation, creating unintended side effects and potential concurrency/race concerns.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client reuses I18n.t('user.email.invalid') for all rejected emails, discarding the server's distinct 'user.email.blocked' reason so blacklist-domain rejections show the wrong message

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, once an email is rejected by the server it is pushed into `rejectedEmails` (on `result.errors.email`), and subsequent `emailValidation` for that same value always fails with `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`. The server now produces distinct email errors via `EmailValidator` (`user.email.not_allowed` and the new `user.email.blocked`), exposed in `users_controller.rb` as `errors: user.errors.to_hash`, but the client discards the specific reason and replaces it with the generic `'user.email.invalid'`, causing blocked/not_allowed emails to show the wrong message after the first failure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmails table and model have no writer path (no admin UI, API, rake task, or seed), so the feature is dead code in production

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `BlockedEmail` (model + migration) and enforces it in `EmailValidator` via `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, but the diff does not add any way to create/manage `blocked_emails` records in production (no controller/admin UI/API/rake/seed changes shown). Without an external writer path, the table will remain empty and the blocking behavior will never trigger, making the added feature effectively inert unless populated manually.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail lookup is case-sensitive, regressing the previous case-insensitive domain-blacklist behavior and allowing easy bypass
Migrated whitelist/blacklist logic in EmailValidator has zero spec coverage for whitelist-rejection, whitelist-acceptance, blacklist-rejection, and blacklist-bypass

adjudication.rationale: The new `EmailValidator#validate_each` includes domain whitelist/blacklist logic based on `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` / `email_domains_blacklist` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb), migrated out of `User#email_validator` which was removed. The added spec (spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb) only tests the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` branch via stubbing and does not exercise any whitelist/blacklist acceptance/rejection/bypass cases, so the finding about zero coverage for those scenarios is accurate and specific to this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: New error-payload contract (errors hash + values object) between UsersController#create and create_account_controller.js has no spec or client test, so key-shape changes silently degrade rejectedEmails behavior

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new JSON error payload from `UsersController#create` (`errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice(...)`) and new client-side logic in `create_account_controller.js` that depends on this shape (`if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values) { ... pushObject(result.values.email) }`). The added specs cover `EmailValidator` and `BlockedEmail`, but there is no controller/request spec asserting the JSON keys (`errors`/`values`) nor any client-side test asserting the rejectedEmails behavior, so this new cross-layer contract could regress silently.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No verification that user.attributes.slice(...) is safe when attributes are nil on the anonymous-create path

adjudication.rationale: In the failure render path, the diff shows `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`. Given `user` is being validated (referenced just above via `user.errors.full_messages` and `user.errors.to_hash`), `user` must be a User instance, and `user.attributes` in Rails is a Hash (not nil) even for unsaved/invalid records. The diff does not show any “anonymous-create path” where `user` or `user.attributes` could be nil, so the concern is not grounded in this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: should_block? performs a DB read-modify-write inside model validation, inflating match_count and last_match_at on every validation attempt rather than real signup attempts

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the method does a `where(...).first` and, when a record exists, increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and `save`s **every time it is called** (even if `action_type` is `:do_nothing`). This method is invoked from `EmailValidator#validate_each` during model validation (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`), so merely running validations (not necessarily a successful/committed signup) will mutate `blocked_emails` statistics. That’s a concrete side effect/perf/metrics concern introduced by the diff, though it may be intentional rather than a functional correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client shows generic 'user.email.invalid' message for blocked emails instead of a blocked-specific message

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, when an email is in `rejectedEmails`, the validator always returns `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` (generic) regardless of the actual server-side email error. The list is populated on create failure for any `result.errors.email` (`rejectedEmails.pushObject(result.values.email)`), including the new blocked-email case added via `EmailValidator` (`record.errors.add(... 'user.email.blocked')`). Therefore blocked emails will be surfaced client-side as `user.email.invalid` instead of a blocked-specific message.

adjudication_records.issue_text: rejectedEmails list is never cleared per-email or on modal close, causing stale cached rejections even after an admin unblocks the address server-side

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a client-side cache `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` and makes `emailValidation` immediately fail if `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` (create_account_controller.js). Emails are added on failed account creation (`pushObject(result.values.email)` when `result.errors.email`), but there is no code in the diff to ever remove entries or reset `rejectedEmails`. Therefore, during the lifetime of that controller instance, an email that was once rejected will stay rejected client-side even if the server-side condition changes (e.g., the email gets unblocked), matching the finding’s “stale cached rejections” concern (the “on modal close” part isn’t shown, but lack of any reset/removal is verifiable).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Blocked-emails feature is inert: no writer path (admin UI, API, rake task, seed, or import) exists to create BlockedEmail records, so the table cannot be populated in production and the feature silently no-ops

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `BlockedEmail` (model + migration) and uses it in `EmailValidator` via `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, but the diff does not add any creation/management path (no controller/admin UI/API/task/seed) to insert rows into `blocked_emails`. As a result, unless records are added out-of-band (manual DB/console), the new blocking behavior will never trigger and will effectively no-op. This is a completeness/product concern rather than a verifiable correctness bug in the code shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail.should_block? uses case-sensitive exact string matching, allowing blocked emails to bypass validation via case variation like Spam@EVIL.com
should_block? performs a write (incrementing match_count and saving) inside model validation, inflating match_count/last_match_at per validation pass and adding an UPDATE to the hot signup path

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `EmailValidator#validate_each` calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` when no other email error exists (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a DB write whenever a matching record exists (`record.match_count += 1`, `record.last_match_at = ...`, `record.save` in app/models/blocked_email.rb). Because validations can run multiple times in a request/lifecycle, this can inflate `match_count/last_match_at` per validation pass and adds an UPDATE to the signup/user validation path. This is a real perf/architecture concern, but not necessarily a functional defect in user signup itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Refactoring email validations in user.rb made presence and uniqueness checks conditional on email_changed?, weakening previously unconditional invariants and allowing an unchanged-but-cleared email to persist

adjudication.rationale: The diff does not make presence/uniqueness conditional on `email_changed?`. It replaces `validates_presence_of :email` and `validates_uniqueness_of :email` with `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true`, which remain unconditional. Only the new custom validator (`validates :email, email: true`) is gated by `if: :email_changed?`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: should_block? performs a read-modify-write incrementing match_count inside model validation, causing double-counting when valid? and save both run validation, and silently mutating stats on read-only validation paths

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb, validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) during validation. BlockedEmail.should_block? (app/models/blocked_email.rb) does a read-modify-write: increments match_count, sets last_match_at, and saves. That means merely running validations (e.g., calling valid? without persisting the User) will mutate blocked_emails stats, and repeated validation passes can increment multiple times. The diff doesn’t show an actual call sequence proving double-counting in practice, but the side-effectful DB write inside validation is clearly present and can skew match_count/last_match_at depending on how validations are invoked.

adjudication_records.issue_text: match_count += 1 is a lost-update race: concurrent signups with the same blocked email can lose increments due to no atomic UPDATE or FOR UPDATE guard

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, when a matching record is found it performs a read-modify-write (`record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = ...; record.save`). Under concurrent signups for the same `email`, two processes can read the same `match_count` value and both save `+1`, losing one increment (no `UPDATE match_count = match_count + 1`, `increment_counter`, or row lock/`FOR UPDATE`). This is a real lost-update race affecting persisted statistics (`match_count` / `last_match_at`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Blocked email lookup is exact case-sensitive match against raw user input with no normalization, so entries stored with different casing (e.g. Spammer@Example.com) fail to block signups
matched_golden_ids: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same vulnerability: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a case-sensitive email lookup without normalization, so changing the email’s casing (e.g., User@Example.com vs user@example.com) can bypass an intended block.

adjudication_records.issue_text: blocked_emails table and model have no writer anywhere in the diff (no admin UI, API, rake task, or seed), so the blocking feature is unusable by operators without manual console inserts

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `blocked_emails` table (migration) and `BlockedEmail` model plus logic that consults it (`BlockedEmail.should_block?` from `EmailValidator`), but there is no code in the diff that creates/manages `BlockedEmail` records (no admin/controller endpoints, rake task, seed, etc.). That means the feature is effectively inert unless operators manually insert rows (e.g., via console/SQL). This is an incompleteness/operability concern rather than a correctness bug in the shown code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client-side rejectedEmails sentinel conflates any email error (including 'email has already been taken') with blocked-email rejection, permanently showing the email as invalid with blocked styling until page reload

Email validation guard is under-scoped: validates with if: :email_changed? means code paths where email_changed? is false (update_column, mass updates, admin edit, invite, SSO) bypass the blocked check entirely

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show the email validator (now `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` in `app/models/user.rb`) only runs when `email_changed?` is true, so the blocked-email check inside `EmailValidator` is likewise conditional. However, the finding’s specific claims about bypass via `update_column`, mass updates, admin edit, invite, and SSO are not verifiable from this diff, and `update_column` would bypass validations regardless of the `if: :email_changed?` guard. Also, the prior implementation already scoped email validation with `if: :email_changed?`, so this is not clearly a defect newly introduced/exposed by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client adds email to rejectedEmails for any server-side email error, not just blocked errors, causing subsequent validations to show generic 'invalid' message instead of the actual server message (e.g., 'already taken')

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, any failed account creation where `result.errors.email` is present causes `result.values.email` to be pushed into `rejectedEmails` (no check for a specific error type). Later, `emailMatch` immediately fails for any email in `rejectedEmails` and returns a generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, overriding more specific server-side reasons (e.g., uniqueness/"already taken", domain not allowed, blocked) for subsequent attempts with the same email.

adjudication_records.issue_text: For genuinely blocked emails, client discards the server's specific reason and substitutes generic user.email.invalid message, making blocked and typo'd emails indistinguishable in the form

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, once an email is added to `rejectedEmails` (on any server-side email error via `if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values) { ... pushObject(result.values.email) }`), the email validation short-circuits and returns `failed: true` with `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`. This ignores the server-provided specific email error (e.g. `user.email.blocked` from the new `EmailValidator`) and makes blocked-vs-other email errors indistinguishable in the field validation UI.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Blocked email check inside EmailValidator is gated by if: :email_changed?, so blocked emails pass validation when email is unchanged, narrowing enforcement without documented intent

adjudication.rationale: In user.rb the new validator is wired as `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, so the BlockedEmail check inside `EmailValidator` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) only runs when `email_changed?` is true. This means a user who already has a now-blocked email can still save the record (e.g., profile updates) without triggering the blocked-email error unless they change the email. The diff doesn’t document whether that limited enforcement is intended, but the behavior is verifiably true from the code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Replacing validates_presence_of/uniqueness_of with a single validates call gates presence and uniqueness on email_changed?, removing the unconditional presence/uniqueness guarantee for unchanged emails

adjudication.rationale: In app/models/user.rb, presence/uniqueness are not gated on email_changed?. The diff replaces `validates_presence_of :email` and `validates_uniqueness_of :email` with `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` (unconditional). Only the custom email validator is conditional: `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Case-sensitive blocklist lookup in BlockedEmail.where(email: email) allows blocked emails to be bypassed by capitalizing letters; emails must be normalized (downcased/stripped) at lookup and insertion

adjudication.rationale: `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` does an exact-match lookup (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`) and the new `EmailValidator` passes the raw `value` through unchanged. There is no normalization (e.g., `strip`/`downcase`) on insertion (`validates :email, ...` only) or lookup, so in a case-sensitive DB (e.g., Postgres) a blocked entry like `bad@spam.com` can be bypassed with `Bad@Spam.com`. The client-side `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` check is also case-sensitive and would miss variants.

adjudication_records.issue_text: should_block? performs a DB read-modify-write (incrementing match_count and saving) inside model validation, enabling unauthenticated write amplification with no rate-limit guard on POST /users

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a DB write during validation: `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb), and `should_block?` does a `where(...).first` followed by `match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, and `record.save` when a matching `blocked_emails` row exists (app/models/blocked_email.rb). This runs as part of `User` email validation on create (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` in app/models/user.rb) and thus is reachable via user signup (`UsersController#create`). That makes repeated unauthenticated signup attempts with a blocked email cause repeated writes/increments with no rate-limit/guard shown in the diff, matching the finding’s write-amplification concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Counter write happens even when other validations fail, so requests creating no account still write to blocked_emails table

adjudication.rationale: The new EmailValidator triggers `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` whenever there are no prior email-specific errors (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a write side-effect by incrementing `match_count`, setting `last_match_at`, and `record.save` when a record exists (app/models/blocked_email.rb). Model validations run even if other fields (e.g., password/username) fail, so a failed signup can still update `blocked_emails` despite no account being created.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Validation can run multiple times per request lifecycle (e.g., valid? called twice), double-incrementing counters

adjudication.rationale: `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb), and `should_block?` has side effects: it increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and saves whenever a record exists (app/models/blocked_email.rb). If a `User` instance is validated more than once (e.g., `valid?` called and later `save` triggers validation again), the same email can cause multiple increments within a single request/flow, inflating the counters and updating timestamps multiple times for one logical attempt.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Whitelist/blacklist regex uses substring matching with no anchor or domain-boundary check, so a whitelist entry like @good.com matches anywhere in the string allowing bypass (e.g., user@evil.com@good.com.fake.tld)
matched_golden_ids: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same core flaw: the email domain whitelist/blacklist regex is not properly anchored/boundary-checked, so it can match a whitelisted domain as a substring/suffix within a larger, attacker-controlled domain (e.g., subdomains or crafted strings), enabling whitelist bypass.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Setting value is interpolated into Regexp.new with only dots escaped, allowing regex metacharacters like (, ), {, * to cause ReDoS or malformed-pattern exceptions

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb#email_in_restriction_setting?`, the code builds a regex with `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` where `domains` is derived from `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist` and only `.` is escaped via `setting.gsub('.', '\\.');`. Other regex metacharacters in the setting (e.g., `(`, `)`, `*`, `{`) are not escaped, which can cause malformed-pattern exceptions or potentially expensive regex behavior. This is directly present in the diff (even if similar logic existed before).

adjudication_records.issue_text: EmailValidator whitelist/blacklist logic migrated from User has zero test coverage; spec only stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and never exercises email_domains_whitelist, email_domains_blacklist, or domain-regex escaping branches

adjudication.rationale: The diff moves the email domain whitelist/blacklist logic out of `User#email_validator` (removed in `app/models/user.rb`) into the new `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` (`SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` / `email_domains_blacklist` branches plus `email_in_restriction_setting?` regex building). However, `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` only tests the blocked-email path by stubbing `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and never sets/varies the SiteSettings or exercises the whitelist/blacklist branches or the regex escaping (`setting.gsub('.', '\.')`). So the migrated logic is effectively untested in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Blocked-path tests are tautological against a stub; side-effecting BlockedEmail.should_block? (increments match_count and saves record on every validation attempt including failed/repeat retries) is never tested through the validator

adjudication.rationale: The validator spec stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` in both examples (`BlockedEmail.stubs(:should_block?).with(record.email).returns(...)`), so it only asserts that an error is/ isn’t added, not the real integration behavior. Meanwhile `BlockedEmail.should_block?` in the diff is explicitly side-effecting (increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and `save`s on every match) and `EmailValidator#validate_each` will call it whenever whitelist/blacklist checks didn’t already add an error (`if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`). That side-effecting path is not exercised through the validator in tests (it’s only tested directly in `blocked_email_spec.rb`), so the finding is a concrete test/coverage concern grounded in the diff, not a functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: record.errors[attribute].blank? guard is untested; no spec constructs a case where domain-restriction already added an error AND email is blocked, so a flipped boolean adding a wrong second error message would ship silently

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb, the blocked-email check is conditional on `record.errors[attribute].blank?` before calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` and adding the `user.email.blocked` error. The added spec (spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb) only stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` true/false and does not set up a case where the whitelist/blacklist logic already added `user.email.not_allowed` while `should_block?` would also be true. That interaction (the guard preventing a second error message) is new nontrivial logic and currently untested, so a regression like flipping the boolean could slip through.

adjudication_records.issue_text: New rejectedEmails client-side blocking flow (users_controller + create_account_controller) has no tests anywhere in the diff; payload contract between symbol-keyed errors hash and JS check on result.errors.email may silently never fire, and rejectedEmails dependent-key invalidation/early-return in emailValidation are unverified

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new client-side rejectedEmails flow in `create_account_controller.js` (tracking rejected emails, early-return in `emailValidation`, and dependent key `rejectedEmails.@each`) and a new server JSON contract in `users_controller.rb` (`errors: user.errors.to_hash`, `values: user.attributes.slice(...)`). The added specs only cover `BlockedEmail` and `EmailValidator`; there are no tests verifying (a) the `/users` create failure payload shape consumed by JS (`result.errors.email` + `result.values.email`), or (b) that changes to `rejectedEmails` actually invalidate/recompute `emailValidation` and block a resubmission of the same email. This is a concrete, diff-grounded gap in coverage for newly added behavior, though the claimed payload mismatch is not provably broken from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail#should_block? performs DB writes (match_count/last_match_at updates via record.save) inside validation, which commits even when the surrounding user save fails, inflating statistics outside the failed transaction

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `BlockedEmail.should_block?` doing side-effecting writes (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`) in `app/models/blocked_email.rb`, and it is invoked from `EmailValidator#validate_each` during user validation (`lib/validators/email_validator.rb`). That means validation can mutate/persist `BlockedEmail` statistics even if the user record ultimately isn’t created/updated. However, the claim that it definitively “commits even when the surrounding user save fails” can’t be proven from this diff alone (it depends on transactional behavior around `user.save`), so this is best treated as a concrete design/architecture concern rather than a verified correctness bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail save errors (e.g. unique-index race under concurrent validation of the same email) raise inside validation, turning a normal signup into a 500 with no retryable path; counter should be incremented after the user save commits

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `BlockedEmail.should_block?` only updates an existing `BlockedEmail` row (`where(...).first` then `record.save`); it does not create rows, so a “unique-index race under concurrent validation of the same email” is not evidenced here. Also it uses `save` (not `save!`), which generally does not raise on validation failure, so the claim that save errors will raise inside validation and turn signup into a 500 is not supported by the shown code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail email matching is case-sensitive (exact-byte where clause) while the legacy blacklist/whitelist regex was case-insensitive, so differently-cased emails like SPAM@X.COM bypass the block

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the lookup is `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, which is an exact string match at the DB level (e.g., case-sensitive on common DBs like Postgres). By contrast, the domain restriction regex in `EmailValidator#email_in_restriction_setting?` is explicitly case-insensitive (`Regexp.new(..., true)`). The diff does not show any normalization (e.g., downcasing) of `value` before calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, so it’s a concrete edge-case risk that blocked emails stored in one casing may not match differently-cased input, though whether this is exploitable depends on normalization elsewhere not shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Nothing in the migration, model, or seed path normalizes case when populating blocked_emails, breaking the backfill/import contract; lookup should downcase both sides and the unique index should enforce it

adjudication.rationale: BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) does an exact match lookup (`where(email: email).first`) and the migration/index store `t.string :email` with a plain unique index. There is no downcasing/normalization on insert or lookup, so `blocked_emails` entries like `Bad@Spam.com` won’t match `bad@spam.com` (and vice versa), and duplicates differing only by case can coexist in Postgres despite the “unique” index. This can cause blocked emails to not be blocked in real use.

adjudication_records.issue_text: users_controller returns user-controlled email in result.values which the frontend permanently blacklists client-side, showing user.email.invalid for that exact string even when the server-side error was different (not_allowed or uniqueness)

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, any signup failure that includes `result.errors.email` causes the submitted email (`result.values.email` from `users_controller.rb`) to be pushed into `rejectedEmails`. Subsequent `emailValidation` checks short-circuit on `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and return `failed: true` with reason `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, regardless of the original server-side error (e.g. `user.email.not_allowed`, uniqueness, or the new `user.email.blocked`). This effectively blacklists that exact user-provided email for the lifetime of the controller and shows a generic/mismatched error message.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Read-modify-write increment of match_count loses increments under concurrency (last writer wins); should use an atomic UPDATE like update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, ...")

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the code does a read-modify-write (`record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = ...; record.save`). Under concurrent calls for the same `email`, two processes can read the same `match_count` and both save `+1`, losing one increment (last writer wins). An atomic SQL update (e.g., `update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...")`) would avoid this lost update.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails whenever any email error (including uniqueness 'already taken') is present, permanently showing 'invalid' message and blocking retry of that email even after correcting a different field

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, any failed account creation response that includes `result.errors.email` causes the submitted email to be pushed into `rejectedEmails` (`pushObject(result.values.email)`). The `emailValidation` computed then short-circuits: if `rejectedEmails.contains(email)`, it returns a failed validation with the generic reason `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, without re-checking server-side or preserving the specific server error (e.g., uniqueness/already taken, blocked, not_allowed). This means that for the remainder of the modal lifetime, re-entering that same email will be immediately marked “invalid” and cannot surface the real error or allow a retry flow for that email within the client.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail.should_block? discards the return value of record.save, so failed writes (lost-update race on match_count, lock timeout) silently drop statistics with no logging

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, when a matching record is found it increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and calls `record.save` but does not check the boolean return value or handle failures (no retry/logging) before returning the block decision (`record && record.action_type == actions[:block]`). This could silently fail to persist the statistics updates, but the diff doesn’t show that these stats are relied on for correctness beyond tracking, so it’s more a robustness/observability concern than a definite functional bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Side-effectful DB write on every validation attempt inflates match_count and performs unguarded writes on a read path for repeated form submits, admin email edits, and retries after other validation failures

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a DB write as a side effect of validation: `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb), and `should_block?` increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and `record.save` whenever a matching record exists (app/models/blocked_email.rb). This will happen on every validation where the email attribute itself has no prior errors (it does not guard on other model errors), so repeated form submits / retries can inflate `match_count` and add write load in what is otherwise a read/validation path. This is a real, diff-grounded concern but not a clearly incorrect behavior given the apparent intent to track matches.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Email validator's nil handling depends on presence validation firing before the each-validator; any refactor reordering validations would pass nil through email_in_restriction_setting? (latent coupling)

adjudication.rationale: In `EmailValidator#validate_each`, passing a nil `value` into `email_in_restriction_setting?` is safe: it only does `value =~ regexp`, and in Ruby `nil =~ /re/` returns `nil` (no exception). Likewise `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` handles nil (`where(email: nil)` is valid). So the diff does not show a correctness defect that depends on presence validation running first; at most it could add an extra `not_allowed` error alongside `presence`, but there’s no demonstrated breakage or order-dependent nil crash.
